Republication Debate
ree-pub-li-KAY-shun
noun phrase (covenant theology debate)
The intra-Reformed debate over whether the covenant of works was in some sense republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai. The republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant included a republication of the works principle (in some formulation); the anti-republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant was an administration of the covenant of grace without a works-principle republication.

Biblical Definition

The intra-Reformed debate over whether, and in what sense, the covenant of works was republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai. The debate concerns the precise relationship between the Mosaic covenant and the covenant of works / covenant of grace. The republication position (held by some in the older Reformed tradition and revived in contemporary discussion, notably by some at Westminster Seminary California) holds that the Mosaic covenant, while an administration of the covenant of grace at the level of eternal salvation, included in some sense a republication of the works principle (do this and live, Leviticus 18:5) — whether with respect to Israel's tenure in the land (a national, typological works-principle governing Israel's temporal blessing and curse in Canaan) or in some other formulation. The republication position appeals to the Pauline contrast between the law and the promise (Galatians 3; Romans 10:5 citing Leviticus 18:5 as the law-principle), the Sinai covenant's conditional blessing-and-curse structure (Deuteronomy 27-28), and the older Reformed sources that spoke of the law as a republication of the covenant of works in some sense. The anti-republication position (held by other contemporary Reformed theologians) holds that the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace, with the law functioning pedagogically (driving to Christ) and normatively (the rule of grateful obedience) but without a works-principle republication; this position emphasizes the gracious character of the Sinai covenant (the LORD redeemed Israel from Egypt before giving the law, Exodus 20:2) and warns that the republication position risks compromising the unity of the covenant of grace. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the republication debate as a substantive intra-Reformed discussion; both positions are held within the confessional Reformed tradition with substantive theological integrity, and the debate concerns the precise formulation of the Mosaic covenant's relationship to the works and grace principles, not a gospel-essential disagreement.

Webster 1828 Definition

Intra-Reformed debate over whether the covenant of works was republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai; the republication position holds a works-principle republication (notably regarding Israel's land tenure); the anti-republication position holds the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace.

REPUBLICATION DEBATE, n. phr. (covenant theology debate) Whether, and in what sense, the covenant of works was republished in the Mosaic covenant at Sinai. Republication position (older Reformed sources; contemporary Westminster Seminary California): the Mosaic covenant, while an administration of the covenant of grace at the level of eternal salvation, included a republication of the works principle (do this and live, Leviticus 18:5) — notably regarding Israel's tenure in the land (a national typological works-principle governing temporal blessing and curse). Appeals to Galatians 3; Romans 10:5; Deuteronomy 27-28. Anti-republication position: the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace; the law functions pedagogically and normatively without a works-principle republication; emphasizes the gracious character of Sinai (Exodus 20:2).

Key Scripture

Leviticus 18:5 — "Ye shall therefore keep my statutes, and my judgments: which if a man do, he shall live in them: I am the LORD."

Exodus 20:2 — "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage."

Galatians 3:17-18 — "And this I say, that the covenant, that was confirmed before of God in Christ, the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after, cannot disannul, that it should make the promise of none effect. For if the inheritance be of the law, it is no more of promise: but God gave it to Abraham by promise."

Deuteronomy 30:15-16 — "See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil... I command thee this day to love the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments."

Modern Corruption

The republication debate is a substantive intra-Reformed discussion; both positions are held within the confessional Reformed tradition with substantive theological integrity; it concerns the precise formulation of the Mosaic covenant, not a gospel-essential disagreement.

expand to see more

Republication as a covenant-theological debate does not undergo lexical corruption. The debate is a substantive intra-Reformed discussion over the precise relationship between the Mosaic covenant and the works and grace principles. The republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant included a works-principle republication in some sense (notably regarding Israel's typological tenure in the land); the anti-republication position holds that the Mosaic covenant was wholly an administration of the covenant of grace. The patriarchal-Reformed reader engages the debate with appropriate care: both positions are held within the confessional Reformed tradition with substantive theological integrity; the debate concerns the precise formulation of the Mosaic covenant's relationship to the works and grace principles, not a gospel-essential disagreement; both positions affirm the substantive unity of the covenant of grace, justification by faith alone, and the imputed righteousness of Christ. The substantive concern in the debate is to honor both the gracious character of the Sinai covenant (the LORD redeemed Israel before giving the law) and the genuine works-principle dimension that Paul identifies in the law (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3). The patriarchal-Reformed reader holds his position with conviction while recognizing the substantive integrity of the alternative within the confessional Reformed tradition.

Hebrew Roots

Intra-Reformed debate over the republication of the covenant of works in the Mosaic covenant; republication vs. anti-republication positions; both within the confessional Reformed tradition.
